sections_target.text: Disassemble Valve Position Lever and Coupling

There are two configurations of valve position levers and couplings used on stop 
valves to ensure positive valve closing the hydraulic piston shaft is usually 
preadded you must release this loading by loosening the coupling bolts in the 
coupling. The bolts are usually long enough to relive this pressure.

Disassemble the valve position lever and 
coupling. The mechanical hydraulic control ( MHC ) figure 17 design configuration comes 
apart easily after the bolts removed. The electro hydraulic control ( EHC ) 
figure 18 design requires jacking up the spring retainer under the spring to remove the 
split washer. With the washer removed, the spring tension will be released up 
on removal of the jacking device.

sections_target.text: Remove Valve Steam Bushing Assembly
Unlock the jam nuts.
Loosen all pull down ring bolts
Rotate off pull down ring.

Attach rigging, using the three eyebolt hole in 
the top of the valve disk.

Use a chain fall to make the vertical lift. Don't use the crane until the guide 
bushing is out of its valve body seat.

The valve stem will rise freely until the stem makes contact with its back seat. 
Continue applying vertical pressure. If this pressure does not break the bushing 
assembly from the housing, it will be necessary to use a jack.
Place the jack between the hydraulic actuator and the valve stem.

sections_target.text: Disassemble Valve Steam Bushing Assembly

Remove the main valve disc cover bolts. These 
are staked.
Lubricate the heads with oil.

Twist the bolts past the penning. The cover will come of easily once the bolts 
are removed. The pilot valve and bypass valve will almost fall out without the 
cover to hold them in place.

Push the valve stem up into the main valve disk until the split washer holding 
the stem to the disk can be removed.

Push the stem in the opposite direction. This will remove the stem from the 
valve disk and expose an anti rotation pin in the stem.
Remove the anti rotation pin and continue sliding the valve stem out of the bushing assembly.

Valve Stems 
Sheet no.2 MRDS

Stems must be non destructively tested during valve component 
inspection.

Check the valves steam 
for cracks, using the red dye method whenever valves are disassembled for 
maintenance. The areas most likely to have cracks are locations such as anti rotation pin holes keyways, the roots of threads, and the inside area of 
corner fillets, particularly in the stem seal area. Generally, cracks along 
the stem axis will not be serious enough to cause scrapping of the stem 
scrapping the stem is only necessary when stem cracks are large and open .

Stop valve steam erosion 
has been reported on many main stop valves designed for full arc admission 
operation. The erosion takes place in a region just below the by pass valve 
disk and is caused by solid oxide particles in the steam. The amount of erosion 
varies greatly from one turbine to another and is a function of the steam coming 
from the boiler.

Valve stems should also be visually 
inspected to :

* Galling. 
 * Excessive oxide chipping or build up.
* Foreign object damage. * Pounding out of stem seal.
* Chipped worn or deformed threads.

Ultrasonic 
Testing of Steam Valve Studs after Period of Service 
Sheet no. 6 MRDS

Tests should be performed by well trained and 
properly qualified personnel.

Perform tests while the studs are in place and generally, after 
the cover has been removed. However where the end of the stud protrudes above 
the nut , the studs may be tested without disassembly.

Use Sperry reflect scope, type UR or equivalent. 
The ultrasonic instrument vertical presentation shall be linear within 
 5 percent of the full scale deflection.

The exposed end of each stud should be free of 
all scale and oxide. Caution should be exercised to maintain a flat surface for 
search unit contact.
Use suitable compliant, such as SAE 20 oil.

Adjust the distance calibration markers on a 
calibration bar of material similar to that of the studs, for accurate distance 
measurements.

sections_target.text: Cam Shafts

The Cam shaft should be inspected for run out and 
journal surface condition. Take micrometer readings, note journal size 
variations, and compare these measurements to the original shaft size and to 
the measurements recorded on the last service report. The following three
faders will determine if shaft replacement is necessary:

With Teflon bearings, the shaft should hold 
taper and shaft roundness to 0.0015 inch on all journals. Depending on the 
wear patter non the bearing journal irregularities may be increased to 0.003 inch.

With grease lubricated brass or bronze bearings, 
shaft irregularities tend to stabilize with tapers and out of round 
conditions in journal areas near 0.008 inch units have been found with taper 
and out of round conditions in journal areas as large as 0.0221 inch.

Graphite impregnated bearings hold tolerances 
some where between the Teflon and greased bearing types. Due to the unusual 
torque loading on cam shafts during operation, you should recommend changing 
shafts whenever the journal surfaces will cause new bearings to wear so that 
they will fit the poor shaft conditions.
